topic.title: The farewell email
topic.claim: The nicest things your company will ever say about you are in replies to your farewell email.
topic.moment: 'Will miss you so much, you were the backbone of this team' from someone who never replied to your messages.

turn.actually: Praise is free once you're leaving, because it can no longer cost anyone a rating or a raise.

topic.because: While you stay, praise has to be paid for in money and promotions. On your last day it costs nothing.
topic.payoff: If they only called you the backbone on your way out, they knew it all along.
topic.behaviour: Colleagues reply-all with warm tributes to someone whose appraisal they rated average.
topic.mechanism: Praise has a price only while it can turn into a raise.
topic.group: Anyone who has switched jobs at least once
topic.send_to: The friend serving notice period right now.
topic.why_now: Job-switch season is constant, and everyone has read or written one of these recently.

score.why: Farewell praise is free because it can no longer cost a rating or a raise. It's dry, human and shareable.

topic.villain: a rating system where praise is free only once you can no longer be rated

cover.headline: Your farewell email gets the [best review of your career]
cover.sub: It arrives on the one day it can't count.

paragraphs: Your farewell email gets the best review of your career.
slides.why_swipe: Why would the best review come after you've already left?

paragraphs: It's your last day. The access card goes back at six, the laptop bag already feels lighter, and the farewell mail sits in Drafts.
The AC hums over a half-empty floor. You hit send at 4:47. The replies start before your chai goes cold.
"Will miss you so much. You were the backbone of this team." It's from someone who was always too busy to answer your Teams messages.
Your phone buzzes against the desk so often it rattles the pen stand.
It feels like honesty at last. You're leaving, nothing is at stake, so why would anyone fake it now?
slides.why_swipe: If they thought it all along, where was it before today?

paragraphs: Your last appraisal said "meets expectations". The comment box had one line: "Good team player." Backbone never made it into that form.
There, it would have cost someone. In most offices a top rating means your manager arguing for you, and a slot someone else doesn't get.
**While you stay, a compliment can turn into money. On your last day, it can't.**
slides.why_swipe: And whose farewell did you reply to like this?

paragraphs: And you've done it too. "Huge loss for the team", typed in ten seconds for someone you watched carry a project all year.
You knew. You'd known for months. You just never said it anywhere it could cost a rating.
slides.why_swipe: So who's still replying after you've gone?

paragraphs: At nine, someone replies-all "All the best!!" to a login that no longer opens.
**The one person who had a form for all this replies with a thumbs up.**

end.save: Read it again the evening your farewell thread starts filling up.
end.send: Send to the friend serving notice period right now, before they read too much into the reply-alls.

draft.caption: What's the most generous line someone wrote in your farewell thread, and did they ever say it to your face before that?
draft.alt_text: A six-slide carousel arguing that your farewell email gets the best review of your career, on the one day it can't count for anything. On your last day, over the hum of a half-empty floor, you send the farewell mail and replies pour in. A colleague who was always too busy to answer your messages calls you the backbone of the team, and it feels like honesty at last. But your last appraisal said 'meets expectations' with a one-line comment, because in most offices a top rating means your manager arguing for you and a slot someone else doesn't get. While you stay, praise can turn into money; on your last day it can't. You have done the same, typing 'Huge loss for the team' for someone you watched carry a project all year, knowing their worth but never saying it where it could cost a rating. It ends with someone replying 'All the best!!' to a login that no longer opens, while the one person who had a form for all this replies with a thumbs up.
